This research aims to investigate the effect of technology use on adolescent well-being. Previous research has relied on Likert scale self-report measures to enumerate adolescents’ technology use. We will complement and extend this research by examining both adolescent self-report technology use using Likert scales and by completing time use diaries. These time use diaries allow for a more detailed investigation of the technology-wellbeing relationship, as we examine not only the total time spent using technology but also the timings of this use. We want to note that our study is correlational and therefore does not have strict independent/dependent variables. Our explanatory variables, however, concern an adolescent’s technology use. We use 4 different measurements. 

1. Self-report technology use: four eight-point Likert scale questions about hours per weekday spent “watching television programmes or films”, spent “playing electronic games on a computer of games system”. “spent using the internet” in a home setting or spent “on social networking or messaging sites or apps on the internet” (1= none, 8 = 7 hours or more). We take the mean of these measures. 

We also use measures that are calculated using data provided by a child using a time use diary. Each child is randomly assigned a weekend day and weekday to complete a time use diary on paper, on the computer or on their phone. They fill out how much time they spend each day doing a variety of activities, in 10 minute slots. We sum the time they report spending with technology:
 - Answering emails, instant messaging and texting
 - Browsing and updating social networking sites (e.g. Twitter, Facebook, BBM, Snapchat)
 - General internet browsing, programming (not time on social networking sites) 
 - Playing electronic games and apps
 - Watching TV, DVDs and downloaded videos

Due to an anticipated negative skew of time use distributions we will create two variables that reflect technology use. We also create 2 dichotomous variables: whether or not the adolescent reported using technology 30 minutes or 1 hour before their reported bedtime. The bedtime is inferred as the time the adolescent reports their activity as ‘sleep’ in the evening of their time use diary completion day. Two types of well-being measures were included in the MCS dataset for each adolescent. There are indicators completed by cohort members, and others completed by their primary caretakers. We will examine a subset of these measures to allow for comparisons between datasets (we are also analysing the Growing up in Ireland and the Panel Study of Income Dynamics US; we do not pre-register these analyses as the datasets are already openly available). 

1. Self-esteem: Adolescents complete 5 items from an abbreviated Rosenberg self-esteem scale: “On the whole, I am satisfied with myself”, “I feel I have a number of good qualities”, “I am able to do things as well as most other people”, “I am a person of value”, “I feel good about myself” (1 = strongly agree to 4 = strongly disagree). Individual scores will be computed for each participant by taking the latent factor of the positively worded items and the reverse-coded negatively worded items. 

2. Short mood and feelings questionnaire: Adolescents are also asked twelve questions that consider their affective state and mood (Angold, Costello, Messer, & Pickles, 1995): “For each question please select the answer which reflects how you have been feeling or acting in the past two weeks:”, “I felt miserable or unhappy”, “I didn’t enjoy anything at all”, “I felt so tired I just sat around and did nothing”, “I was very restless”, “I felt I was no good any more”, “I cried a lot”, “I found it hard to think properly or concentrate”, “I hated myself”, “I was a bad person”, “I felt lonely”, “I thought nobody really loved me”, “I thought I could never be as good as other kids”, “I did everything wrong” (1 = not true, 2 = sometimes, 3 = true). Individual scores will be computed for each participant by taking the latent factor of the positively worded items and the reverse-coded negatively worded items.

3. Caretakers fill out the common Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ; Goodman, Ford, Simmons, Gatward, & Meltzer, 2000). The SDQ is popular, and has been used to assess adolescents in schools, clinical settings and schools from diverse backgrounds (Goodman, 2001). It encompasses 25 questions, five each about prosocial behaviour, hyperactivity or inattention, emotional symptoms, conduct problems and peer relationship problems (0 = not true, 1 = somewhat true, 2 = certainly true). Individual scores will be computed for each participant by taking the latent factor of the positively worded items and the reverse-coded negatively worded items. The latent factor will be constructed by loading the four sub-scales of the SDQ (emotional, peer problems, hyperactivity, conduct problems) on four latent factors separately, and then loading them onto a general factor. We do not include pro-sociality in the analyses as this is routinely excluded in previous studies.

We analyse the data using lavaan and SEM. We first run a specification curve analysis which runs each possible analysis that is possible using our pre-specified analytical decisions. These analytical decisions are: which technology use measure we use (5 options), which well-being measure we use (3 options), whether we include controls (2 options, yes/no) and whether technology use is on a weekday or weekend (2 options). 

We run each model by extracting the relevant latent factor for well-being and correlating it with the chosen technology use measure. We either filter the data to only include weekend or weekday measures and either include controls or not in our model. After running each possible analysis, we plot these to show the general trend of results. 

To test each hypothesis separately we then run a series of permutation tests. We select all specifications that include the technology use variables addressed in the hypotheses (H1 = self-report Likert scale, H2 = continuous time diary, H3 = 30 minutes before bedtime, H4 = 1 hour before bedtime), and then run a permutation test on these, checking whether the original data results in more significant p values than scrambled datasets where we know the null effect is true.

Data from 18 participants has been collected in a pilot phase to determine whether people are willing to wait 30 seconds at the end of the experiment in return for seeing the balloon's limit. Counterfactual Curiosity - One-shot Task

This experiment is a follow-up to the five experiments reported in our pre-print "The Lure of Counterfactual Curiosity" (DOI: https://doi.org/10.31219/osf.io/jm3uc). These studies address the question of whether people seek post-decision counterfactual information - how much they could have won - in a gambling task (the Balloon Analogue Risk Task, BART; Lejuez et al., 2002). In previous studies we used a within-participant design, presenting participants with 60 trials of the BART and giving them the option to view the balloon's limit after each trial. Participants frequently sought information even at some cost even though a. it made them feel bad, and b. (we argue that) it had no instrumental value. Our argument that the information had no instrumental value relied on the independent nature of the trials in the task - since the balloon's limit was randomly determined on each trial - so gaining information about the limit on the previous trial cannot benefit performance on future trials. However, it may be argued that participants believe that there is some non-random structure that can be learned through seeking information about the balloon's limit. Thus, they might have sought information for instrumental reasons, even though the information was actually not of any instrumental value. 

In the current study, we aim to demonstrate that people will still incur costs to learn post-decision counterfactual information when the possibility to use that information in the future is completely removed because there is only one trial and that information still makes them feel bad. In the new version of the task, participants practice by completing 10 trials of the BART with no option to seek information. They rate their emotions on a visual analogue scale after seeing the outcome of each trial. 

After the 10 practice trials, participants receive the following instructions: "Now that you've had a chance to practice, it's time for the real thing! There is one more round and this time each pump is worth 20p!". They then complete one critical round of the BART. If participants 'go bust' on this final round, then they do not get a bonus payment and they are not offered the opportunity to see how far they could have gone. If they 'banked' the money, then after rating their emotions about the outcome, then they are given the following instructions: "You won £X.XX. Would you like to see how much you could have won if you kept going? The information comes at a price - you will have to wait 30 seconds for your completion code at the end of the experiment! Press Y for yes or N for no.". 

If they choose to see the information, then they see an animation of the balloon inflating to its randomly determined limit and are presented with information about how much money they could have won on the trial. If they choose not to receive the information then they continue to observe their obtained outcome for the same time as if they had chosen to view the information. Participants then rate their emotions a second time. This second emotion rating is the critical dependent variable.

This experiment is a follow-up to the five experiments reported in our pre-print \"The Lure of Counterfactual Curiosity\" (DOI: https://doi.org/10.31219/osf.io/jm3uc). These studies address the question of whether people seek post-decision counterfactual information - how much they could have won - in a gambling task (the Balloon Analogue Risk Task, BART; Lejuez et al., 2002). In previous studies we used a within-participant design, presenting participants with 60 trials of the BART and giving them the option to view the balloon's limit after each trial. Participants frequently sought information even at some cost even though a. it made them feel bad, and b. (we argue that) it had no instrumental value. Our argument that the information had no instrumental value relied on the independent nature of the trials in the task - since the balloon's limit was randomly determined on each trial - so gaining information about the limit on the previous trial cannot benefit performance on future trials. However, it may be argued that participants believe that there is some non-random structure that can be learned through seeking information about the balloon's limit. Thus, they might have sought information for instrumental reasons, even though the information was actually not of any instrumental value.

In the current study, we aim to demonstrate that people will still incur costs to learn post-decision counterfactual information when the possibility to use that information in the future is completely removed because there is only one trial and that information still makes them feel bad. In the new version of the task, participants practice by completing 10 trials of the BART with no option to seek information. They rate their emotions on a visual analogue scale after seeing the outcome of each trial.
